title: Symphony No. 2 in D major
hook: Begun in an Italian winter, heard in Finland as a song of freedom.

painting.title: Study from Koli
painting.pairingNote: Rocks, pines and Lake Pielisjärvi seen from the Koli heights, painted by Sibelius’s brother-in-law: the Finnish landscape that Finns have long heard in this symphony.

facts: Sibelius began the symphony in 1901 in Rapallo, on the Italian coast, where his friend Baron Axel Carpelan had raised the money for him to spend the winter. He finished it in Finland early in 1902.

He conducted the first performance himself in Helsinki on 8 March 1902. It was a great success. He then revised it, and the revised version was first played in Stockholm on 10 November 1903, conducted by his brother-in-law Armas Järnefelt.

Finland was then ruled by Russia, and Finnish language and culture were under pressure. Many listeners heard the grand finale as a picture of the struggle for independence, and the work was even called the “Symphony of Independence”. Whether Sibelius meant it that way is still debated.
The symphony grows from tiny cells. A three-note rising figure heard at the very start returns in many disguises, and becomes the great theme of the finale.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a pastoral morning that keeps breaking into fragments (I), a dark, troubled ballad (II), a furious scherzo that runs without a break (III) into a triumphant finale (IV).

movements.heading: Allegretto
movements.summary: It begins like a fresh spring morning, with a gentle pulse in the strings and a cheerful tune in the woodwinds. Then the music does something unusual: instead of building long themes, Sibelius throws out short fragments, lets them fall silent, and gradually fits them together. Only at the climax do the pieces lock into a whole.

mainIdeas.name: The pulse
mainIdeas.description: the strings repeat a soft, rising three-note figure, like breathing.

mainIdeas.name: The woodwind tune
mainIdeas.description: a bright, folk-like melody for oboes and clarinets.

mainIdeas.name: The horn call
mainIdeas.description: a soft, warm answer from the horns.

stops.hear: The strings pulse gently on rising three-note chords
stops.happening: The three-note cell from which the whole symphony grows

stops.hear: The oboes and clarinets play a bright, dancing tune; the horns answer softly
stops.happening: The first theme group: several short ideas, not one long tune

stops.hear: A woodwind holds one long note, then plunges downwards; the strings pluck underneath
stops.happening: The second group, made of fragments with silences between them

stops.hear: The brass rise in a short, proud phrase, then the music thins out again
Fragments are passed around the orchestra, growing tenser
The music surges to a broad climax with blazing brass; the opening ideas return on top of it

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The gentle pulse in the strings comes back, and the movement fades out

notice: Listen to the opening pulse in the strings. The same three rising notes, made much bigger, become the main theme of the finale.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: George Szell recorded the symphony in November 1964 with the Concertgebouw Orchestra in Amsterdam, for Philips, as a guest conductor; his own orchestra was in Cleveland. The Spotify album holds the symphony alone, in four tracks. The third track ends where the music runs on into the finale.

movements.heading: Tempo andante, ma rubato
movements.summary: A dark ballad with sudden storms. It opens with a long, plucked walk in the low strings, over which the bassoons sing a mournful tune. Twice the music builds to a violent climax, and twice it is answered by a calm, glowing melody in a far-off key. In a sketch for this music Sibelius wrote of a stranger who turns out to be Death.

mainIdeas.name: The walking bass
mainIdeas.description: a long line plucked by the double basses and cellos.

mainIdeas.name: The bassoon theme
mainIdeas.description: a sad, low melody, first played by two bassoons.

mainIdeas.name: The consolation
mainIdeas.description: a soft, radiant melody in F-sharp major for the strings, marked “Christus” in Sibelius’s sketch.

stops.hear: A soft drum roll, then the low strings pluck a slow, walking line
Two bassoons play a sad, low melody over the plucked strings
stops.happening: The first theme, in D minor

stops.hear: The music grows restless and breaks into a fierce outburst for the brass
Silence, then the strings play a soft, glowing melody, very slowly
stops.happening: The second theme, in F-sharp major (*Andante sostenuto*)

stops.hear: The dark music returns, more agitated than before
A second, even bigger climax, with full brass
The glowing string melody again, now in a new key

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The music gathers itself once more and ends with hard, loud chords

notice: Notice how the movement keeps changing speed. Sibelius marks it *rubato*: [[rubato|rubato]] means the players may stretch and push the tempo, and here the whole orchestra does.

movements.heading: Vivacissimo – Lento e suave
movements.summary: A furious, breathless [[scherzo|scherzo]], with the strings racing in fast repeated notes. Twice it stops dead for a slow, tender oboe melody. After the second time the music does not return to the scherzo: it climbs, slowly and steadily, straight into the finale without a break.

mainIdeas.name: The scherzo
mainIdeas.description: whirling, rapid notes in the strings, with sharp accents from the woodwinds.

mainIdeas.name: The oboe tune
mainIdeas.description: a slow, gentle melody that begins on a single repeated note.

stops.hear: The strings race in fast, nervous notes; the woodwinds snap at them
Everything stops; a solo oboe plays a slow, tender melody, starting on one note repeated again and again
stops.happening: The [[trio|trio]], in G-flat major (*Lento e suave*)

stops.hear: A trumpet blast, and the racing strings are back
The slow oboe melody again

stops.label: Last 90 seconds
stops.hear: The music begins to climb; a short phrase is repeated, higher and louder each time
stops.happening: The bridge to the finale: there is no break

notice: Listen to the end of this track and the start of the next as one. The third movement does not finish; it opens into the finale.

movements.heading: Finale: Allegro moderato
movements.summary: The arrival. A broad, rising theme in D major, answered by trumpet calls, bursts in at the end of the long climb. Its opposite is a long, mournful passage in which a scale keeps turning over in the low strings while the woodwinds lament. The two alternate, until the mournful music itself is turned into the final blaze.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a broad, rising melody in the strings, built from the three-note cell of the first movement, with trumpet fanfares in reply.

mainIdeas.name: The second theme
mainIdeas.description: a scale figure going round and round in the violas and cellos, under a sad melody in the woodwinds.

stops.hear: The full orchestra arrives on a broad, rising melody; trumpets answer with fanfares
stops.happening: The main theme, in D major

stops.hear: Quiet: the lower strings turn a scale over and over; a sad woodwind melody floats above
The scale figure builds to a powerful climax
Calmer; the themes are broken up and combined
The broad main theme returns
The turning scale again, now starting very softly and growing for minutes on end
stops.happening: The longest build of the symphony

stops.hear: The mournful theme is transformed into a radiant hymn for the brass in D major

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Long, held chords for the whole orchestra

notice: Follow the turning scale in the low strings in the long build. It hardly changes; everything above it does.

threads.title: From fragments to a whole
threads.body: Sibelius builds his themes from small cells and lets them come together slowly. The rising three-note figure from the first bar becomes the big tune of the finale.

threads.title: Darkness and light
threads.body: The storms of the slow movement and the lament of the finale are answered by the D major blaze at the end.

threads.title: No break
threads.body: The scherzo runs straight into the finale, as in Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony, so that the last two movements are heard as one long climb.

threads.title: Italy and Finland
threads.body: The first ideas came in Rapallo; the work became, in Finland, a symbol of hope during years of Russian pressure.
